issues.question: What burdens and patent-validity presumption govern the prohibition application?

answer_groups.answer: The applicants bear the legal burden of proving validity throughout. The respondent need only adduce evidence capable of putting invalidity in play, at which point the validity presumption is spent.

answer_evidence_quotes: the legal burden remains with the first person throughout the proceedings and does not shift to the second person.
evidence which is sufficient to put the allegations of invalidity “in play” and which is not clearly incapable of establishing those allegations.

issues.question: Were the disclaimers relating to the patent valid?

answer_groups.answer: Yes. The applicants established that the allegation challenging the disclaimers was unsubstantiated.

answer_evidence_quotes: Taking the whole of the evidence into account, on the balance of probabilities standard, I conclude that the applicants have met their burden to demonstrate that this allegation is unsubstantiated.

issues.question: Was the patent invalid for obviousness?

answer_groups.answer: No. The applicants proved that the obviousness allegation was unsubstantiated.

answer_evidence_quotes: I therefore find that on the totality of the evidence the applicants have proven on a balance of probabilities that the respondent’s allegation of invalidity on the basis of obviousness is unsubstantiated.

issues.question: Was the patent invalid because the claimed use was only an old product or process?

answer_groups.answer: No. The patent claimed a new use of sildenafil for treating erectile dysfunction, not merely an old product or a new process for an old product.

answer_evidence_quotes: It is not a new process for an old product they discovered but an entirely new use.

issues.question: Were the claims broader than the invention made or disclosed?

answer_groups.answer: No. A skilled reader would understand the claims as treating the symptoms of erectile dysfunction, so the breadth allegation was unsubstantiated.

answer_evidence_quotes: I think a skilled reader would have read the Patent as indicating a treatment for ED that was curative or prophylactic in nature with regard to the symptoms of ED.
As such, on a balance of probabilities the applicants have demonstrated that this allegation is unsubstantiated.

issues.question: Did the use claims fail the legislative requirements for listing on the patent register?

answer_groups.answer: No. The claims were for the use of sildenafil as a medicine to treat erectile dysfunction; manufacturing a medicament was secondary, so the eligibility allegation failed.

answer_evidence_quotes: The use being spoken of is therefore the use of sildenafil (which is a medicine, as defined above, i.e. “a substance”) for the curative or prophylactic treatment of erectile dysfunction in man, and the manufacture of a medicament or the adaptation for oral treatment are merely secondary aspects to the essential claimed use.
On the balance of probabilities the applicants have demonstrated that this allegation is unsubstantiated.

target_mentions.evidence_quote: The issue of burden of proof and presumption of validity was recently dealt with by the Court of Appeal in Abbott Laboratories v. Canada (Minister of Health), 2007 FCA 153

The respondent refers to the Supreme Court of Canada decision in Hoffman-La Roche & Co Ltd. v. Commissioner of Patents [1955] S.C.R. 414, 23 C.P.R. 1 at para. 5 (S.C.C.) [Hoffman], cited positively by the Federal Court in Abbott Laboratories v. Canada 2005 FC 1332, 45 C.P.R. (4th) 81 at para. 58 (F.C.), aff’d 2007 FCA 153 at paras. 11-14 [Abbott Laboratories 2005].

target_treatments.label: applied
target_treatments.evidence_quote: In that case the Court of Appeal found at paragraph 9 that “[i]t is now beyond debate that an applicant for a prohibition order under the NOC Regulations bears the burden of establishing its entitlement to the order”
target_treatments.target_proposition_as_characterized: An applicant for a prohibition order bears the burden of establishing entitlement to the order, subject to the evidentiary treatment of the validity presumption.

answer_groups.answer: No. The judge wrongly confined the analysis to the draft CRO instead of examining the parties' communications, so the matter had to be remitted.

issues.question: What role does Sattva play in the contractual dispute?

answer_groups.answer: Sattva governs interpretation of contract terms, including use of the factual matrix, but does not determine whether a contract exists in the first place.

answer_evidence_quotes: I note that Sattva does not apply to determine whether a contract exists, but rather to interpret the terms of the contract.

target_mentions.evidence_quote: Referring to the law set out in Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp., 2014 SCC 53, it was put this way in her factum:

target_treatments.label: distinguished
target_treatments.evidence_quote: I note that Sattva does not apply to determine whether a contract exists, but rather to interpret the terms of the contract.
target_treatments.target_proposition_as_characterized: Sattva supports using the factual matrix to interpret a contract after existence is established; it does not resolve contract formation.

issues.question: Was the complaint filed within the statutory six-month period?

answer_groups.answer: Yes. The complaint was filed within six months of the settlement-stage events that completed the grievance process.

answer_evidence_quotes: the Tribunal finds that the complaint dated November 15, 2004 was properly filed within the six-month time limit as required in subsection 53(2) of the Act.

issues.question: Did the copyright-related dispute arise under the scale agreement and fall within the Writers Guild's exclusive bargaining authority?

answer_groups.answer: Yes. Acquisition and distribution rights were matters of scale-agreement interpretation, and the Writers Guild was the exclusive bargaining agent for the grievance.

answer_evidence_quotes: the Tribunal finds the dispute concerning the acquisition and distribution of rights is a matter related to the interpretation of the scale agreement.
the Tribunal finds that the matter falls within the ambit of the scale agreement and that the WGC is the exclusive bargaining agent to deal with any grievance arising out of the scale agreement.

issues.question: Did the Writers Guild breach its duty of fair representation through bad faith or arbitrary conduct?

answer_groups.answer: It did not act in bad faith, but its failure to answer repeated information requests on a critical issue was arbitrary and breached the duty of fair representation.

answer_evidence_quotes: the Tribunal finds that the WGC did not act in bad faith in its representation of the complainant.

this failure to properly address the clearly articulated concerns of the complainant, unintended as that failure may have been on the part of the WGC, nevertheless amounts in our view to arbitrary conduct.

issues.question: What remedy followed from the fair-representation breach?

answer_groups.answer: Only declaratory relief was appropriate; the complainant's requested directions did not flow from the statutory breach.

answer_evidence_quotes: The Tribunal finds that the remedies requested by the complainant do not flow from a violation of section 35 of the Act.
the Tribunal finds that the declaratory relief as stated above is the appropriate disposition to deal with the matters at issue.

issues.question: Did the contracts contain more favourable terms for further use of the scripts than the scale agreement?

answer_groups.answer: No. The contracts did not specify more favourable terms for further use or renewal.

answer_evidence_quotes: there were no terms specified in the complainant's contracts with the CBC concerning further use of the dramatic scripts that were more favourable than those contained in the agreement.
